name: heldout-o1js
label_provenance: Labels were written by reading each contract's source against o1js semantics and recorded in this file BEFORE o1js-scan was run on any of these repositories. They are predictions, not scanner output. They are NOT third-party labels — see the limitations section of README.md.
inclusion_criteria: Listed in MinaFoundation/list-of-projects (the ecosystem's own index), so selection is not ours.
Contains at least one `class ... extends SmartContract` with `@method`, outside test and node_modules paths.
Not present in docs/mina_calibration.md — the calibration corpus was used to tune rules and is not held out.
exclusion_criteria: Pre-o1js `snarkyjs`-era contracts. The analyzer documents keying on the modern require* precondition API and the o1js decorator forms; scoring it on a 2022 API would measure the wrong thing. Ten candidate repos were excluded on this basis and are listed under `excluded`.
Repositories with no SmartContract source (frontends, backends, SDK wrappers).

cases.label: vulnerable
cases.reasoning: withdraw() sends a fixed 2 MINA to `this.receiverPublicKey.get()` with no authorization and no precondition on the read. setReceiver()/setSender() let any caller overwrite those addresses from an unconstrained @method argument, so anyone can point the escrow at themselves and drain it. Expect a HIGH missing-precondition on the bare .get() and unconstrained-witness findings on the setters.
cases.notes: The same EscrowContract is vendored four times (ui/src, whisper-key-core/src, api/src/deployer, plus a build copy). Counted as one case; duplicate findings are expected and are not scored separately.
cases.label_correction: The original label also expected O1JS_MISSING_STATE_PRECONDITION on withdraw(). That was MY error, found when the scanner did not fire: whisper-key-core/src/EscrowContract.ts:19 does carry a precondition (`this.receiverPublicKey.assertEquals(this.receiverPublicKey.get())`, the legacy spelling). I had read the ui/src copy and assumed a bare get(). The scanner was right and the label was wrong. Corrected after the run, which is recorded here because it weakens this expectation as a blind prediction.

cases.label: vulnerable
cases.reasoning: initialize() writes symbol/decimals/maxSupply/owner with no precondition that the contract is uninitialized, so any caller can re-initialize and take ownership. Ownership is then checked with `this.owner.getAndAssertEquals().assertEquals(this.sender)` on o1js 0.15, where bare `this.sender` is not signature-constrained, so the check is prover-chosen on both sides.
known_defects_not_expressible: Re-initialisation / ownership takeover: no rule models 'a state write that should be one-shot'.
Legacy bare `this.sender` used as an authorization subject. O1JS_UNCONSTRAINED_SENDER matches `this.sender.getUnconstrained()`, the modern spelling, so the 0.15-era form is expected to be missed.
cases.status_reason: The *Proof false-positive fix in 0.19.0 was developed against this case, so under the anti-overfitting rule it is no longer held out. It stays in the corpus as a regression case; the next benchmark version must not count it as unseen evidence.

cases.label: vulnerable
cases.reasoning: faucet(toAddress) mints 50,000 tokens to any caller-supplied address with no authorization. setElectionDetails() sets two preconditions on the same property with different arguments (getAndAssertEquals() then assertEquals(empty)), which is the V-O1J-VUL-012 shape in the legacy spelling.
known_defects_not_expressible: Unauthorized mint: no rule models mint authorization; O1JS_UNCONSTRAINED_RECIPIENT covers send recipients only.

Precondition overwrite in the legacy `assertEquals` spelling. O1JS_PRECONDITION_OVERWRITTEN deliberately matches only require* because assertEquals is overwhelmingly the in-circuit Field assertion, so this real instance is expected to be missed.

cases.label: vulnerable
cases.reasoning: Uses this.sender.getUnconstrained() in airdrop claim and factory fee paths, and sets account permissions explicitly in several contracts. Expect unconstrained-sender findings and permission findings; severity depends on whether a signature is required on the same account update.
cases.notes: Largest case in the corpus (1864 contract lines). Reviewed at method-effect granularity, not exhaustively.

cases.label: vulnerable
cases.reasoning: updateRoot() writes an unconstrained @method argument straight to the commitment state. The write is gated by proving knowledge of a private key, so real impact is admin-scoped, but the witness-to-state-write finding is correct and expected.
known_defects_not_expressible: A PrivateKey is taken as a @method parameter, so the key becomes part of the witness. No rule models this.

cases.label: clean
cases.reasoning: submitRepeaterSolution() calls zkProgram.verify() before reading its public input, and asserts the step count. submitStillSolution() constrains every board cell to 0 or 1 and checks the transition. The contract holds no state and moves no funds, so there is nothing for a witness to reach. Negative case: any HIGH or MEDIUM finding here is a false positive.

label_corrections_note: One expectation was corrected after the first run — see whisper-key-escrow. Corrections made after seeing scanner output are recorded inline rather than silently applied, because a label edited to match the tool is not evidence.

status_semantics.held-out: Never used to develop, tune, or debug the scanner. Only these cases are evidence about unseen code.
status_semantics.development: A change was built against this case, so it is no longer unseen. It stays in the corpus as a regression case and must carry a status_reason naming the change. Counting it as held-out evidence again would be overfitting.
status_semantics.regression: Retained only to pin behaviour that a past change established. Not evidence in either direction, and must carry a status_reason.

status_counts_note: Declared rather than derived so that moving a case out of held-out has to be an explicit edit. tests/test_heldout_manifest.py recomputes these and fails on a mismatch, which is what stops the held-out count from drifting upward by accident.
benchmark_version_note: v1 froze six held-out cases at 0.18.0. v2 records that usdm-token-owner moved to development status after a fix was built against it. Five cases remain genuinely unseen.
